source_text: Ἡ μὲν οὖν ἀνθρωπίνη ἐγκράτεια, ἡ κατὰ τοὺς φιλοσόφους λέγω τοὺς Ἑλλήνων, τὸ διαμάχεσθαι τῇ ἐπιθυμίᾳ καὶ μὴ ἐξυπηρετεῖν αὐτῇ εἰς τὰ ἔργα ἐπαγγέλλεται· ἡ καθ’ ἡμᾶς δὲ τὸ μὴ ἐπιθυμεῖν, οὐχ ἵνα τις ἐπιθυμῶν καρτερῇ, ἀλλ’ ὅπως καὶ τοῦ ἐπιθυμεῖν ἐγκρατεύηται. λαβεῖν δὲ ἄλλως οὐκ ἔστι τὴν ἐγκράτειαν ταύτην ἢ χάριτι τοῦ θεοῦ. διὰ τοῦτο εἶπεν «αἰτεῖτε καὶ δοθήσεται ὑμῖν».
pass_a_gloss: Human continence among the Greek philosophers promises fighting desire and not serving it in deeds; ours is not-desiring — not that one desiring should endure, but that he be continent even of desiring. This continence cannot be taken otherwise than by the grace of God; therefore he said, Ask and it will be given you.
pass_b_english: Among the Greek philosophers, human self-control claims to fight desire and not to serve it in deeds. Among us it is not to desire at all — not that someone who desires should merely tough it out, but that he should be continent even of desiring. And this self-control cannot be received in any other way than by the grace of God. That is why he said, “Ask, and it will be given you.”

choices.why: Grace is the only way this Christian continence is received.

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the distinction between the philosophers' definition of continence (fighting desire) and the Christian definition (being continent even of the desire itself). The scripture citation 'Ask and it will be given you' correctly corresponds to the Greek 'αἰτεῖτε καὶ δοθήσεται ὑμῖν'.
